Here's my feedback. It's hard to communicate this in writing without sounding direct and harsh - apologize if this is how it comes across. I know I was pissed off when I received this feedback. This is what FAANG is expecting though. 
 
1) Cut out: Expertise & Tools. I don't think calling out Slack or Teams adds value to a professional TPM resume. 
2) Put the timelines of each position and compaby name on the same line as the title (save 2 lines) 
3) Remove Technical Program Manage from main title of the first page - save two lines 
4) Squeeze the NY in the personal info section at the top to the line above - save a line 
5) Remove big Experience section header, the reader knows what it is - save three lines 
6) Limit each Bullet in the experience section to 2 rows max. Bonus points for squeezing into one row. It's possible 
7) The focus of each bullet in the experience section should be on your __impact __to the company. Preferably with numbers to show how you influenced the bottom line. For example: "worked on building a PHP to manage the order of workflow" --> "Improved the order workflow by X% (days/HP/customer satisfaction) by rewriting legacy PHP code" 
8) Remove descriptions of what you were responsible for, the reader knows what TPMs and SDEs are resposible for. 
9) Computer Programmer --> Software Development Engineer 
 
Now, you should be able to fit it on one page.

## Resume Prompts

> You are an expert resume writer with over 20 years of experience working with job seekers trying to land a role in `[industry]`.

>

We are navigating some trickiness here because there is a bunch of overlap. "Project" management is often viewed as a subset of the broader "Program" management skillset. Generally, the more complex and ambiguous the initiative, the more it will lean toward "Program" management.

I probably oversimplified in my description above of the difference between the two. There can certainly be some ambiguity while handling project management at the higher levels. It's the degree and type of ambiguity that really starts differentiating. 

Ambiguity I would consider "project management": There's a set of security vulnerabilities in 3P libraries we have been recently made aware of. We need to fix these across the entire company, but we don't know which teams need to do work. How do we roll this out?

Ambiguity I would consider"program management": This security vulnerability is systemic in how our technical architecture operates today. How can we continue to operate a live site and meet our functional and non-functional requirements while completely changing the underlying architecture? What technical tradeoffs or compromises can we make, based on our understanding of the intersection of the technical and business requirements?

* As AG said, you should condense this down. My standard reminder is that a hiring manager has 60-120 seconds to read your resume. When you have more words, that doesn't mean they spend more time reading. It means each word is read with less care. Focus your words to what matters. 

* You have bullet points under your name, a professional summary, core competencies, detailed bullet points per job, AND a Technical Exposure section? You've repeated "DC Build & Commissioning" 7 times in this resume. 

* In general, your professional experience bullet points show that you were entrusted with work on a real scale. It's good to demonstrate scale. * Explain as if folks are unfamiliar with your work. You're burdened with the Curse of Knowledge. You know what ByteDance owns. I know what ByteDance owns. But does every hiring manager and recruiting coordinator reading this resume know what ByteDance owns? No. Demonstrate the complexity by showing off what all these PoPs are actually used for.
